newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordanian gunman says Israeli girls mocked him.
newsitem.headline: Jordanian gunman says Israeli girls mocked him.

text.p: A Jordanian soldier who gunned down seven Israeli schoolgirls harboured deep anti-Israeli feelings but opened fire "on the spur of the moment" because the girls mocked him while he prayed, his lawyer said on Thursday.

"I heard laughter and jeers and girls mocking me when I ended my prayers...I was outraged by one girl taking pictures and other girls laughing at me," Jordanian Sergeant Ahmed al-Daqamsa was quoted by lawyer Ahmad Najdawi as saying.

Najdawi is the first lawyer allowed to see Daqamsa since he emptied the clip of his rifle on March 13 at the girls on a school trip to Baqoura, a Jordanian border territory leased to Israel under the 1994 peace treaty.
Daqamsa told Najdawi in the headquarters of Jordan's military intelligence, where the soldier has been under interrogation since the shooting, that he acted impulsively.
"It appears that the soldier's motives were patriotic and he acted out of a rage on the spur of the moment," said Najdawi, a prominent lawyer who often defends political activists.
"The man could not control his nerve and took hold of his rifle and started shooting, motivated by all the frustrations and injustice felt by an Arab against Israeli arrogance," Najdawi told Reuters.
"I cannot say he is a hero, but he is a nationalist who acted out of nationalist motives and frustration at what the Arabs are suffering," he added.
King Hussein has expressed remorse over the killing and branded it as a "vile criminal act". Last week he rebuked Daqamsa's comrades for not shooting him dead on the spot.

But Jordanians privately criticised a high-profile visit by the monarch to pay condolences to the girls' families in Israel as an excessive display of emotion when Israel was preparing to build a new Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem.
Many Jordanians, reflecting hardened anti-Israeli views, say Daqamsa is a hero motivated by a deep sense of outrage over a history of Israeli violence against Palestinians.
Lawyers have come to his defence seeking a public trial and demanding he be treated with the same leniency they say Israel has shown to perpetrators of violence against Arabs.
Najdawi said he found Daqamsa "normal with no signs of being beaten" by his interrogators.
He desribed him as a simple "unpoliticised peasant" who "watched television screens and was filled with a sense of humiliation and helplessness by the treatment of Arabs by Israelis."

Asked about reports that Daqamsa was mentally unstable, Najdawi said he saw no proof of any abnormal behaviour but he might request the soldier be referred for medical examination when his trial begins.
Daqamsa also denied that he was prompted by others to gun down the girls, Najdawi said, adding he expected the trial to start as soon as his interrogation came to a close.

Najdawi said the defence would demand a public trial as a main prerequisite for justice to take its course, adding the death sentence in such a case should be waived, as Jordanian law should not be more severe than "Israeli law which abolishes capital punishment for such cases".
